messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 45
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Agricultural Worker
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 48

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Never Alone: make sure never to be alone with another person, Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Marcus is a 45-year-old agricultural worker who lives with his partner in a small rural community. He came to therapy reluctantly, at his partner’s urging, after months of tension and a growing sense that he was losing everything he still cared about. The first time Marcus spoke about what happened to him, he stared at the floor and his voice dropped to a near whisper. He was eight years old when he watched his father beat his mother in the kitchen of their home. He remembered the sound of her body hitting the linoleum, the way his father’s belt buckle caught the light, and the fact that he did nothing. He stood frozen in the doorway, too terrified to move or scream. He has carried that moment with him every day since.

For decades, Marcus tried to push the memory away. He told himself it was over, that he was a child, that there was nothing he could have done. But the harder he tried not to think about it, the more the images would surface at unpredictable times—while he was driving a tractor across a field, or sitting with his partner in the living room, or lying awake in the dark. He learned early that the worst moments came when he was alone. So he made sure never to be. At work, he arranged his schedule so that he always had another person nearby, even if that meant taking longer to finish a job or swapping tasks with a coworker. He would never volunteer for the early-morning irrigation shift that required walking through the orchard by himself. When his supervisor told him he was being reassigned to a solo task, Marcus felt his chest tighten and he found a reason to refuse, not explaining why. Over time, his boss grew frustrated, and Marcus feared he was being seen as difficult or unreliable.

At home, he insisted on keeping lights on in every room until he was ready to sleep, and even then he would leave a hallway light on. His partner noticed that he seemed more on edge after sunset, that he would flinch at the sound of a car door closing or a dog barking outside. Marcus could not explain it—he simply knew that darkness made the world feel dangerous in a way that daylight did not. People told him he was safe, that the man who hurt his mother was long gone, that the house was locked, that nothing was going to happen. But their words never reached that part of him that stayed on guard. He found himself scanning the yard through the window before opening the back door, checking locks twice, and walking through the house with his fists half-clenched. He had come to believe that safety was not something he was allowed to feel.

The guilt was the thing that gnawed at him most. He replayed that kitchen scene again and again, and each time he saw himself standing there, doing nothing. He told himself he would never forgive his own cowardice, even though he knew logically that he had been a child. The anger he could not direct at himself found its way toward his father, even though his father had been dead for fifteen years. Marcus spent hours at night, lying next to his sleeping partner, rehearsing in his mind what he would say if he could confront him, imagining different ways to make him pay. He knew it was pointless, but the rumination felt like the only thing he could control. Meanwhile, the happiness he remembered from his youth—the easy laughter, the sense of possibility—had drained away. He felt hollow, irritable, and convinced that people were not to be trusted. He had pulled back from friendships, stopped attending church, and rarely accepted invitations from extended family. His relationship had become strained because his partner felt shut out, unable to understand why Marcus could never relax, why he always needed company, why he seemed to carry a weight that could not be put down.

What finally brought Marcus to seek help was a moment in the field when a coworker came up behind him without warning and clapped him on the shoulder. Marcus spun around, heart pounding, and nearly shoved the man before he caught himself. He saw the shock and hurt on his colleague’s face, and for the first time he thought: I am not okay. He agreed to see a therapist because his partner said she could not keep living this way, and because he was tired of being afraid in a world that everyone else seemed to find ordinary. He said he did not know if he could ever feel safe, but he wanted to stop feeling so alone even when someone was right beside him.
